name: Trust Signals
description: Visible cues intended to signal safety or legitimacy (third-party trust seals, security badges, credential stacking) can lower perceived risk and increase purchase intent -- but the effect is conditional rather than automatic: it depends on the viewer's own psychological state and on whether the specific seal is one the viewer actually recognizes.
design_relevance_note: The rationale behind stacking security badges, credential logos, and trust seals near a checkout or signup form -- the corpus's own evidence is a useful corrective here: an unrecognized seal does essentially nothing, so the badge itself does less work than the design intuition assumes.
myth_risk_note: Trust-badge stacking is treated as a near-default design pattern, but the corpus's own null-on-average finding (driven by low recognition of most real-world seals) means the pattern often does less than assumed -- a real, checkable gap between design habit and evidence.
prevalence_note: A near-universal checkout/signup-page design habit (badge stacking, security seals), independent of whether the underlying effect is as reliable as the habit assumes.

findings.description: In a 300-subject online lab experiment comparing two real-world third-party trust seals against a no-seal control, third-party seals were NOT effective at increasing purchase probability on average. This null average result was driven entirely by the low-dissemination (poorly recognized) seal; the seal with high real-world dissemination/recognition did produce a positive effect. This is a direct, empirical debunk of the naive practitioner claim that 'adding any trust badge boosts conversion' — effectiveness depends specifically on whether consumers actually recognize the seal.
findings.source_title: Not all seals are equal: An experimental investigation of the effect of third-party seals on purchase probability in electronic commerce

findings.description: Online safety/security cues (e.g. safety-oriented Web content) lower consumers' risk perceptions and produce more favorable attitudes and purchase intentions — but only conditional on the consumer's regulatory focus: the effect appears specifically when consumers are in a prevention (loss-avoidance) focus, not universally. This directly complicates the popular blanket claim that adding a trust/security cue always increases trust or conversion.
findings.source_title: The persuasiveness of online safety cues: The impact of prevention focus compatibility of Web content on consumers' risk perceptions, attitudes, and intentions

applications.title: RocketLawyer.com stacking attorney credentials, press logos, and a security badge
applications.description: RocketLawyer.com combines several distinct authority signals at once -- attorney photos and staff credentials, logos from major news organizations that have covered the company, and a McAfee security badge -- layering expertise, media validation, and technical trust signals together.
applications.ethical_note: Authority signals here point to presumably real, checkable credentials (named attorneys, real press outlets, a known security certification) rather than vague or manufactured claims -- for a service category (legal advice) where verifying real expertise is itself in the user's own interest, this looks like the principle used in its clean form.
